name: Scalability
summary: The ability to keep meeting demand as data volume, concurrency, and load grow by adding more resources rather than rewriting the system.
description: Scalability is how gracefully a data architecture absorbs growth — more rows, more sources, more concurrent queries, more events per second — by adding capacity. Horizontally scalable designs partition work across many nodes and decouple storage from compute so each can grow independently. Poorly scalable designs hit a single-node or single-writer ceiling and require re-architecture instead of more hardware.

mechanisms.name: Data partitioning and sharding
mechanisms.note: Splitting data by key or time range spreads storage and query work across nodes so no single machine is the bottleneck.

mechanisms.name: Decoupled storage and compute
mechanisms.note: Keeping data in object storage and spinning up independent compute lets each dimension scale without moving data.

mechanisms.name: Horizontal scale-out of distributed processing
mechanisms.note: Frameworks that parallelize across a cluster add throughput linearly by adding workers.

mechanisms.name: Consumer groups and partition parallelism
mechanisms.note: Stream consumers scale by adding instances up to the partition count, dividing the load automatically.

mechanisms.name: MPP columnar query engines
mechanisms.note: Massively parallel processing engines fan a single query across many nodes to serve high concurrency over large tables.

manifestations.statement: Open table formats over object storage with elastic Spark/warehouse compute let bronze/silver/gold layers grow to petabytes and add compute per workload independently.
One copy of partitioned Iceberg data in object storage scales storage cheaply while many independent engines scale compute out to match query demand.
Partitioned logs plus consumer-group parallelism scale event throughput by adding partitions and stream workers with no schema-on-write ceiling.
High-volume event ingestion into partitioned columnar stores scales out linearly to absorb traffic spikes across huge cardinality.
Warehouse-native transformation on cloud MPP engines scales concurrency and data volume by resizing or adding virtual warehouses on demand.
Distributed OLAP engines shard data and replicas across nodes to sustain high query concurrency at scale, though very large state can strain rebalancing.
Device fleets fan into partitioned ingest topics and time-partitioned stores, so millions of devices scale by adding brokers and consumers.
Tenant-partitioned schemas or tables scale with tenant count, but a few very large tenants can create hotspots that require per-tenant isolation work.
Dimensional models on an MPP warehouse scale well for reporting, but wide fact-table growth and conformed-dimension rebuilds add coordination cost.
CDC scales with source throughput and warehouse merge capacity, but high-churn tables and single-writer merge targets can become the limiting factor.
Identity resolution and profile unification scale with the warehouse, but graph-style stitching over many sources grows super-linearly with match complexity.
Hub/link/satellite loads parallelize cleanly by pattern, but the many-join query pattern strains at scale and needs marts to stay performant.
Federated queries are bounded by the slowest and least scalable underlying source, so overall scale is capped by whatever leg cannot fan out.
By design this is single-node in-process analytics, so it scales up only to one machine's memory and cores and cannot scale out horizontally.
On-prem source capacity and sync bandwidth cap growth, so scaling often means a hardware refresh rather than adding elastic cloud resources.
Activation throughput is capped by downstream SaaS API rate limits, so the loop cannot scale past what the destination tools accept.
Share-in-place scales to many consumers without cloning data, but concurrent collaborator queries all land on the provider's compute, which becomes the shared ceiling.
Decentralized domain ownership on shared self-serve infrastructure scales organizationally, letting many teams ship data products in parallel without a central bottleneck team.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Scaling out means running more nodes, replicas, and coordination services, so total compute and storage spend climbs even when per-unit efficiency improves.

tradeoffs.title: Consistency
tradeoffs.note: Partitioning and sharding data across nodes weakens cross-shard and global consistency, forcing you to accept eventual or bounded-staleness reads instead of a single authoritative view.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Distributing work introduces cross-node coordination, data shuffling, and network hops that add overhead to each request, so a single query is often slower than on one machine.

tradeoffs.title: Operational complexity
tradeoffs.note: Distributed systems require rebalancing, partition management, and cross-node failure handling that are far harder to run and reason about than a single-node deployment.
